claims.text: Nanocrystalline W38Ta36Cr15V11 develops Cr-V-rich precipitates under energetic-particle exposure near 8 dpa.
The Cr-V-rich precipitates formed near 8 dpa increase hardening in W38Ta36Cr15V11.
Replacing approximately 5 at% Cr with 5 at% Hf will suppress irradiation-induced Cr-V-rich precipitation.
Hf preferentially bonds with Cr in the modified alloy.
Preferential Hf-Cr bonding reduces the amount of free Cr available to form Cr-V-rich precipitates.
Hf addition alters vacancy diffusion involved in irradiation-induced precipitation.
Hf addition alters the nucleation kinetics of Cr-V-rich precipitates.
Suppression of Cr-V-rich precipitation will minimize irradiation-induced hardening.
The Hf substitution will stabilize the tungsten alloy matrix during irradiation.
The Hf-modified alloy will preserve radiation resistance relative to the unmodified alloy.
Adding Hf while reducing Cr will preserve practical bulk manufacturability.
The proposed modified composition is W38Ta36Cr10V11Hf5 in atomic percent.
At 8 dpa and approximately 500°C, W38Ta36Cr10V11Hf5 will contain significantly fewer Cr-V-rich precipitates than W38Ta36Cr15V11.
At 8 dpa and approximately 500°C, W38Ta36Cr10V11Hf5 will have lower hardness than irradiated W38Ta36Cr15V11.
The proposed suppression effect is expected to hold up to 8 dpa over 200–800°C.
The temperature range of 200–800°C is representative of fusion first-wall and divertor conditions.

contradictions.description: The baseline fields say that precipitation increases hardening, whereas the hypothesis frames the baseline property to be preserved as low hardening. These statements are not strictly irreconcilable, but the distinction between absolute hardness and irradiation-induced hardening is left unresolved.
